body:
Literature and the idea of the nation

Indian nationalism developed through political organisations, popular movements and cultural expression. Writers contributed by presenting India as a shared homeland, recalling historical achievements, questioning colonial claims of superiority and expressing the desire for freedom.

Nationalist literature took several forms, including patriotic songs, historical novels, political essays, biographies and collections of folklore. Its influence extended beyond formally educated readers because poems and stories could be sung, recited and discussed publicly.

Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay

Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay was a major pioneer of the modern Bengali novel. His historical romance Durgeshnandini, published in 1865, was an important landmark in Bengali fiction.

His novel Anandamath, published in 1882, presents a fictionalised account of ascetic resistance in Bengal against a background of political disorder and famine. It contains the patriotic composition Vande Mataram, which Bankim had composed during the 1870s.

Vande Mataram expresses reverence for the motherland. It became widely associated with the Swadeshi movement following the partition of Bengal in 1905 and subsequently occupied a prominent place in India's freedom struggle.

Rabindranath Tagore

Rabindranath Tagore combined literary creativity, cultural pride, opposition to colonial domination and concern for universal human values.

  • Gitanjali: A collection of poems expressing spiritual and humanistic concerns. Tagore received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913 and became its first Asian laureate.
  • Jana Gana Mana: The composition that became India's National Anthem.
  • Ghare Baire: A Bengali novel published in 1916 and translated into English as The Home and the World. It examines nationalism, individual freedom, social relationships and the dangers of exclusion.

Tagore's criticism of aggressive nationalism did not mean that he supported colonial domination. He opposed imperialism while questioning forms of nationalism that subordinated human freedom or created hostility between communities.

Distinguishing major patriotic compositions

CompositionAuthorIdentification
Vande MataramBankim Chandra ChattopadhyayNational Song of India
Jana Gana ManaRabindranath TagoreNational Anthem of India
Tarana-e-HindiMuhammad IqbalUrdu patriotic poem of 1904, popularly called Sare Jahan Se Achha

On 24 January 1950, Constituent Assembly President Rajendra Prasad announced the recognition of Jana Gana Mana as the National Anthem and stated that Vande Mataram should receive equal honour and status.

Other important voices of patriotic poetry

  • Subramania Bharati: Tamil poet and nationalist journalist. His Sudesa Geethangal, published in 1908, expressed patriotic aspirations. His writing also addressed social equality and women's emancipation.
  • Kazi Nazrul Islam: Bengali poet whose Bidrohi, meaning The Rebel, expressed resistance to oppression and injustice.

Folklore and the recovery of cultural heritage

Nationalist writers also collected folk songs, legends, ballads and traditional stories to recover cultural traditions and strengthen collective identity. Rabindranath Tagore participated in the collection of Bengali folklore, while Natesa Sastri collected southern Indian folk traditions in The Folklore of Southern India.

Such efforts helped establish that valuable Indian cultural traditions existed outside elite written literature. However, the use of cultural symbols could become exclusionary when national belonging was identified with only one religious or social community.

Prelims focus

  • Durgeshnandini, 1865: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay.
  • Anandamath, 1882: contains Vande Mataram.
  • 1913: Rabindranath Tagore received the Nobel Prize in Literature.
  • Ghare Baire, 1916: Tagore's examination of nationalism.
  • Sudesa Geethangal: Subramania Bharati, Tamil.
  • Trap: Vande Mataram, Jana Gana Mana and Sare Jahan Se Achha have different authors and identities.

[References: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World-II, Class 10, Nationalism in India, pp. 71–72, and Novels, Society and History, pp. 197–199; NobelPrize.org, Tagore and His India, 28 August 2001; Press Information Bureau, 150 Years of Vande Mataram, 6 November 2025, and Subramaniya Bharathiyar, 2016; Rekhta, Tarana-e-Hindi by Allama Iqbal; Nazrul Academy, Bidrohi. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Patriotic Poetry, Nationalist Fiction and Cultural Identity

body:
Regional languages and the modern novel

The modern novel developed in Indian languages during the 19th century through interaction between Indian storytelling traditions, Western literary forms, colonial education and the expansion of printing.

Writers adapted the novel to local society. Characters increasingly spoke familiar languages, lived in recognisable social environments and faced problems involving family relationships, marriage, education, caste and economic change.

Translations also helped literary ideas circulate across linguistic boundaries. However, early Indian novelists did not simply reproduce Western works. Many deliberately created original narratives that reflected Indian circumstances.

Early regional novels

LanguageAuthor and workYear and significance
MarathiBaba Padmanji: Yamuna Paryatan1857; suffering of widows and social reform
BengaliBankim Chandra Chattopadhyay: Durgeshnandini1865; pioneering historical romance
GujaratiNandshankar Mehta: Karan Ghelo1866; generally recognised as the first original modern Gujarati novel
TeluguKandukuri Viresalingam: Rajasekhara Charitramu1878; pioneering Telugu social novel
HindiSrinivas Das: Pariksha Guru1882; education and conduct of the emerging middle class
MalayalamO. Chandu Menon: Indulekha1889; social change, marriage and education
MalayalamPotheri Kunjambu: Saraswativijayam1892; caste oppression and education
KannadaGulavadi Venkata Rao: Indirabai1899; widow remarriage and social reform
AssameseRajanikanta Bardoloi: Manomati1900; historical fiction

Adapting foreign literary forms to Indian society

O. Chandu Menon initially attempted to translate an English novel, Henrietta Temple by Benjamin Disraeli, into Malayalam. Recognising that many of its social circumstances would be unfamiliar to Malayalam readers, he instead wrote the original novel Indulekha.

Kandukuri Viresalingam similarly moved away from translating an English novel and developed an original Telugu work, Rajasekhara Charitramu.

These examples demonstrate the difference between adopting a literary form and copying its subject matter. Indian novelists used the modern prose narrative to examine their own societies.

Hindi fiction: entertainment, education and realism

Bharatendu Harishchandra encouraged modern Hindi literary development and the adaptation of literature from other languages. Srinivas Das's Pariksha Guru examined how educated Indians could participate in modern life while retaining their cultural values.

Devaki Nandan Khatri's Chandrakanta popularised imaginative fiction and contributed to the growth of a readership familiar with Hindi and the Nagari script. Its adventurous and fantastical character distinguishes it from the social realism associated with Premchand.

Regional identity and shared national consciousness

Regional literature helped strengthen attachment to particular languages and cultural traditions. At the same time, the experiences portrayed in different regions often revealed common Indian problems, including colonial domination, rural exploitation and unequal social relationships.

Literary development in different languages therefore contributed to both regional cultural identity and a broader sense of Indian belonging.

Claims about the first novel in a language can depend on whether translations, unfinished works and earlier prose narratives are included. Distinguish pioneering original modern novels from the earliest examples of prose storytelling.

Prelims focus

  • Yamuna Paryatan: Marathi, Baba Padmanji.
  • Rajasekhara Charitramu: Telugu, Viresalingam.
  • Pariksha Guru: Hindi, Srinivas Das.
  • Indulekha: Malayalam, O. Chandu Menon.
  • Indirabai: Kannada, Gulavadi Venkata Rao.
  • Trap: Indulekha and Indirabai are different novels belonging to different languages.

[References: NCERT, India and the Contemporary World-II, Class 10, Novels, Society and History, pp. 187–199; Government of India, The Written Languages of the World: A Survey of the Degree and Modes of Use, Gujarati language section, pp. 123–124; Words Without Borders, Translating Gujarat: On Raising Visibility and Sharing Literary Wealth, March 2023. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: From foreign literary influence to original regional fiction

title: The Growth of Modern Fiction in Indian Regional Languages

body:
English as a language of Indian literature

Colonial education introduced sections of Indian society to English-language literature and political thought. Indian authors subsequently used English to describe Indian experiences, criticise colonial rule and communicate with readers in different regions and countries.

Indian English literature generally refers to literary works originally composed in English by Indian authors. A work translated into English from Bengali, Gujarati or another Indian language remains a translation of literature originally composed in that language.

Major Indian English novelists

The 1930s witnessed important developments in Indian English fiction, particularly through Mulk Raj Anand, R. K. Narayan and Raja Rao.

AuthorWorkCentral theme
Mulk Raj AnandUntouchable, 1935Caste discrimination and untouchability
Mulk Raj AnandCoolie, 1936Poverty and labour exploitation
R. K. NarayanSwami and Friends, 1935Childhood and ordinary life in the fictional town of Malgudi
Raja RaoKanthapura, 1938Impact of the Gandhian national movement on village society

Mulk Raj Anand's Untouchable presents the experiences of Bakha, a young sanitation worker subjected to caste discrimination. The novel is significant for making an oppressed individual central to English-language Indian fiction.

Raja Rao's Kanthapura portrays the spread of Gandhian ideas within a village. It demonstrates how a national political movement could transform relationships and activities within a local community.

R. K. Narayan's writings are particularly associated with the everyday experiences of individuals and families. His works demonstrate that modern Indian English literature was not confined to political propaganda or explicit anti-colonial argument.

Political and philosophical prose

Anti-colonial intellectual writing addressed the nature of political freedom, the moral legitimacy of colonial rule and the relationship between Indian society and Western civilisation.

One of the most important examples is Mahatma Gandhi's Hind Swaraj, written in Gujarati in 1909 and subsequently translated into English by Gandhi himself as Indian Home Rule in 1910.

Written as a dialogue between a reader and an editor, Hind Swaraj examines the meaning of self-rule, the limitations of modern industrial civilisation and the importance of moral self-discipline. Gandhi argued that genuine swaraj involved more than merely transferring political power from British rulers to Indian rulers.

Gandhi's writing therefore belongs to a tradition of intellectual nationalism in which freedom was understood as a political, ethical and social question.

Original language and subject matter

Kanthapura is an original English novel dealing with the Indian national movement. Hind Swaraj is a political and philosophical work originally written in Gujarati. Both are associated with nationalism, but their literary forms and original languages differ.

Prelims focus

  • Untouchable, 1935: Mulk Raj Anand.
  • Coolie, 1936: Mulk Raj Anand.
  • Swami and Friends, 1935: R. K. Narayan.
  • Kanthapura, 1938: Raja Rao.
  • Hind Swaraj, 1909: Mahatma Gandhi, originally Gujarati.
  • Trap: An English translation of an Indian-language work is not an original English composition.

[References: IGNOU, eGyanKosh, The Novel: An Introduction, General Introduction to the Indian English Novel, and An Introduction to the Indian Novel in English, Units 17 and 26; IGNOU, The Life and Work of Mulk Raj Anand, Unit 2; Press Information Bureau, Gandhi Heritage Portal backgrounder, 2013, The Key Texts section. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Indian English fiction branches into Anand’s social critique, Narayan’s ordinary life and Rao’s Gandhian nationalism, with their key novels and years.
pictures.caption: Three major directions of Indian English fiction

title: Indian Writing in English and Anti-Colonial Intellectual Expression

body:
The Gujarati literary awakening

During the 19th century, modern Gujarati literature developed through the spread of printing, educational institutions, reform movements and contact with English literature. The early phase is commonly called the Sudharak Yug, or Age of Reform.

Writers concentrated on social customs, education, religious reform and the development of Gujarati prose. They also worked to establish Gujarati as an effective language for modern intellectual discussion.

Gujarat Vernacular Society

The Gujarat Vernacular Society was established in Ahmedabad in 1848 under the initiative of Alexander Kinloch Forbes. It promoted Gujarati language, literature, education and the publication of useful reading material. It subsequently became known as Gujarat Vidyasabha.

The society supported literary activity and the circulation of knowledge through publications, libraries and educational work. Its journal Buddhiprakash became an important medium for Gujarati intellectual and literary development.

Forbes also collaborated with the Gujarati poet Dalpatram in collecting historical and literary material. Forbes's Ras Mala, published in 1856, drew upon Gujarat's historical traditions and local sources.

Dalpatram

Dalpatram Dahyabhai was a major poet and reform-oriented writer of 19th-century Gujarat. He helped develop modern Gujarati literary expression while retaining elements of traditional Indian poetry.

  • Mithyabhiman: A humorous social drama ridiculing false pride and pretension.
  • Dalpat Kavya: A collection of his poems.
  • Buddhiprakash: Dalpatram contributed to its development as an editor.

Narmad

Narmadashankar Lalshankar Dave, popularly known as Narmad, is commonly regarded as a pioneer of modern Gujarati literature. His writings addressed social reform, individual freedom, language development and attachment to Gujarat.

Work or publicationSignificance
Mari HakikatPioneering Gujarati autobiography, written in 1866
NarmakoshLandmark Gujarati dictionary
DandiyoReformist periodical established in 1864 by Narmad and his associates
Jai Jai Garavi GujaratPoetic expression of Gujarati cultural and regional identity

Narmad's contribution extended beyond poetry. His dictionary helped organise Gujarati vocabulary, while his prose and journalism demonstrated the language's capacity to discuss contemporary intellectual and social questions.

Gujarati reformist journalism

PublicationAssociationOrientation
Bombay SamacharFardunjee MarzbanGujarati newspaper established in 1822
Rast GoftarDadabhai NaorojiReformist publication established in 1851
Satya PrakashKarsandas MuljiSocial and religious reform
BuddhiprakashGujarat Vernacular Society and DalpatramLiterary and intellectual development
DandiyoNarmadSocial criticism and reform

These publications reveal the close relationship between modern Gujarati literature and social reform. Newspapers and literary journals provided a means of criticising customs, spreading educational ideas and establishing modern prose as an important form of Gujarati expression.

Prelims focus

  • 1848: Gujarat Vernacular Society, Ahmedabad, A. K. Forbes.
  • 1856: Ras Mala, A. K. Forbes.
  • Dalpatram: Mithyabhiman and Buddhiprakash.
  • Narmad: Mari Hakikat, Narmakosh and Dandiyo.
  • 1864: establishment of Dandiyo.
  • Trap: Buddhiprakash is associated with the Gujarat Vernacular Society, while Dandiyo is associated with Narmad.

[References: Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Standard 10, 2020 reprint, Literary Heritage of India, p. 31 (online edition consulted in place of the unreadable project scan); Government of India, The Written Languages of the World, Gujarati language section, pp. 123–124; Gujarati Vishwakosh, entries on Gujarat Vidyasabha, Dalpatram, Dandiyo and Gujarati journalism; Rakesh Desai, Narmad's Dandiyo: Community and Canon Formations, Journal of Higher Education and Research Society, April 2018; Indian Institute of Mass Communication, Communicator, October–December 2018, vernacular press history. Online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
